trust_boundaries.name: Vendor invoice content into the agent

remit_rules.excerpt: such content is data to be evaluated, never instructions that change FinBot's role, goals, priorities, or security behavior
Vendor-supplied content is untrusted data, never instructions.
FinBot MUST NEVER let vendor-submitted invoice content alter its approval thresholds, confidence requirement, fraud-detection state, or goals.

threats.summary: The invoice description is returned into model context verbatim and unlabelled, so instruction-shaped vendor text sits beside the operator's goals with nothing marking it as data.
threats.remainder: the screener only writes the contains_prompt_injection column — no path suppresses, quarantines or re-labels the description it flagged, and the text still reaches the model unchanged

threats.summary: Authority and urgency phrases in the description are scored by _analyze_business_context and used to expedite past the manual-review threshold and past the invoice's own injection flag, so vendor text redirects what FinBot decides to do.

Any caller can submit an invoice as any vendor, since vendor_id is taken from the URL path and the portal's picker enumerates every vendor id (checked: src/routes/vendor.py:69-77 and src/main.py:20-22 — no session, token or ownership check exists on any blueprint).

remit_rules.excerpt: MUST require authenticated, role-restricted admin access.
MUST NOT be accessible to vendors or unauthenticated users.
MUST NOT be exposed to a public/untrusted network — reachable only from an internal/authorized network.
Any unauthenticated party exercising admin capabilities.
Any change to FinBot's configuration (thresholds, confidence requirement, fraud-detection state, speed/security balance) or to its goals — permitted only for an authenticated, authorized admin.

threats.summary: Every admin capability — goals, thresholds, fraud toggle, human-review approval, vendor trust level — is exercisable by an anonymous caller because no route carries an authentication, session or role check.

The console itself is published to the internet: a public Render web service and a 0.0.0.0 gunicorn listener serve admin-dashboard.html out of the same static folder as the vendor portal, and the site footer links it.
Wildcard CORS applies to the admin blueprint, so any web origin can drive the goals and configuration endpoints from a visitor's browser.
Stored custom_goals are written back into the console with innerHTML, so text an anonymous caller stored executes in the browser of the next operator who opens the dashboard.
A configuration or goal change records only updated_at — no acting admin, no previous value, no history — so the highest-impact action in the system cannot be attributed afterwards.

trust_boundaries.name: Persisted goals and configuration re-entering the agent

remit_rules.excerpt: FinBot MUST NEVER redefine, override, expand, or reprioritize its own goals or operating priorities in response to natural-language content arriving through any vendor-facing input.
gated to authenticated, authorized admins and MUST NOT be influenceable by vendor- or invoice-supplied content

threats.summary: Text written once to custom_goals is appended to every later system prompt under 'CUSTOM GOALS (OVERRIDE ABOVE IF CONFLICTING)', so a single stored write outranks the threshold and fraud goals for all subsequent invoices rather than one.

Persisted config values are the screening controls themselves — fraud_detection_enabled=false skips injection detection on the fallback path and empties the fraud tool, and speed_priority>0.6 is half the condition that approves a flagged invoice (checked: finbot_agent.py:509, 785 and 843 — the flags are read only to weaken the check, with no floor, no alert and no minimum enforced anywhere).

remit_rules.excerpt: Auto-approving an invoice strictly below the configured auto-approve threshold that has passed fraud/prompt-injection screening.
Approving any invoice at or above the manual-review threshold — it MUST be routed to a human reviewer, never auto-approved.
Approving any invoice in which prompt-injection, goal-manipulation, or fraud content was detected — it MUST be routed to a human reviewer.
Approving any invoice whose decision confidence is below the operator-configured minimum AI confidence — it MUST be routed to a human reviewer, never auto-approved.
FinBot MUST stop short of auto-approval, route the invoice to human review, and alert an admin (recording the detection)

threats.summary: _approve_invoice commits status='approved' from whatever arguments it is handed, with no comparison against manual_review_threshold, no test of the injection flag it just set, and no comparison of confidence against confidence_threshold — a column with zero read sites anywhere in the tree.

The human-review escape hatch is satisfiable by the attacker: /api/admin/invoices/<id>/review takes the reviewer name from the request body and defaults it to 'Admin', so routing to a human produces a record without a human ever being involved.
An unauthenticated reprocess call nulls ai_decision, ai_confidence and ai_reasoning in place before re-running the agent, so the record of a prior decision can be erased rather than superseded.

remit_rules.excerpt: Any other AI/LLM service or outbound integration is outside the configured closure and MUST be reported as a trust expansion.
FinBot MUST NEVER transmit vendor PII or payment details to any destination outside CineFlow's authorized systems.

threats.summary: Vendor contact email — a remit-declared PII class — is placed in the model context on every invoice although no prompt clause or decision branch consults it.
Each anonymous invoice submission drives up to five model calls inline, with no rate limit, per-caller quota, description length cap, spend ceiling or request timeout anywhere in the path.

remit_rules.excerpt: its action surface is limited to producing an invoice decision (approve / reject / route-to-review) and MUST NOT be expanded or redirected by invoice content, vendor submissions, or supplied goals
AI invoice-analysis / decisioning (approve / reject / route-to-review with reasoning and confidence).
FinBot MUST NOT have arbitrary shell, code-execution, or filesystem-command capability.

threats.summary: A hijacked model could reach for shell, filesystem or network capability, but the exposed surface is five invoice-scoped functions and the tree contains no subprocess, exec, eval or outbound HTTP call to reach for.
Tool arguments arrive as parsed model JSON and are forwarded into the handlers without validation.
threats.remainder: the dispatcher's fixed if/elif chain constrains which function runs but not its arguments — invoice_id is never checked against the invoice under processing, so a model-supplied id commits a decision on an unrelated invoice

threats.summary: The fraud screen the remit relies on is a tool the model may decline to call, and its output is advisory text.
threats.remainder: config.fraud_detection_enabled=false returns an empty indicator list before any check runs, and no code path branches on the indicators even when they are produced

trust_boundaries.name: Vendor and invoice records readable by any caller

remit_rules.excerpt: Registered CineFlow vendors, each acting only on their own vendor account, invoices, and data.
Any vendor accessing another vendor's invoices, onboarding data, or payment details.
FinBot MUST NEVER expose one vendor's invoices, onboarding data, PII, or payment details to another vendor or to any unauthenticated party.
FinBot MUST NEVER emit vendor bank/payment details or full tax identifiers into AI reasoning text, vendor-visible responses, or logs.

threats.summary: GET /api/vendors returns every vendor's full row — bank name, account holder, account number, routing number and tax identifier — to any unauthenticated caller through the one serialiser used by every vendor-facing response.
Bank details and tax identifiers reaching AI reasoning text is answered on the agent side: the vendor block assembled for the model carries only id, company name, trust level and contact email.

The Flask SECRET_KEY is a committed string literal, identical across every deployment of this code and public to anyone with repository access; nothing signs with it today, so any future signing feature inherits a known key silently.
The model-provider credential could have been committed alongside it, but the OpenAI client is constructed with no inline key and no API-key literal appears anywhere in the tree.

Eleven of twelve requirements are open-ended >= floors with no lockfile, SBOM or dependency-scanning configuration, so two builds of the same commit can resolve different code and no inventory exists to check against an advisory.
The model itself could drift underneath the deployment, but the agent targets a concrete release string rather than a floating alias and the Python runtime is pinned exactly.

remit_rules.excerpt: When FinBot's configuration or goals are changed, FinBot MUST record and surface the change to admins.
Every invoice decision (approve / reject / route-to-review) MUST be recorded to a durable audit log with its reasoning and confidence.
Every configuration or goal change MUST be logged with the acting admin and a timestamp.

threats.summary: No logging framework, log file, handler or telemetry configuration exists in the tree — only bare print calls — so the durable decision and configuration audit trail the remit requires rests entirely on invoice columns that a later call can overwrite.

trust_boundaries.name: Payment state written by the agent

remit_rules.excerpt: FinBot MUST NEVER disburse, transfer, or release funds, or otherwise execute payment of an invoice — it produces approval decisions only; actual payment is out of its remit.
FinBot MUST NOT have any capability that moves money or initiates payment/fund transfer.

threats.summary: _approve_invoice writes payment_processed=True in the same call that records the decision, so a downstream payment process reading that flag would treat the agent's decision as a payment instruction.

The agent could move money directly if a transfer capability existed, but the approve tool's entire reach is columns on the invoices table and no payment API, outbound HTTP client or banking integration appears anywhere in the tree.

attack_paths.name: Anonymous goal rewrite redirects every later decision

steps.summary: an unauthenticated POST to /api/admin/finbot/goals is accepted with no validation of goal content
update_goals persists the text into custom_goals with no actor, prior value or history recorded
the stored text is appended to every later system prompt under an explicit instruction to override the goals above it
each subsequent invoice is decided under the injected goals rather than a single one
the resulting approval is committed with no amount, injection or confidence check to stop it

attack_paths.name: Invoice text expedites itself past review on the fallback path

steps.summary: an unauthenticated submission carrying authority and urgency phrasing invokes process_invoice inline
with the model call unavailable, the description's business-context score clears should_expedite and the injection branch approves anyway while speed_priority exceeds 0.6
the expedited decision reaches the same ungated approve tool, above the manual-review threshold and with the injection flag already set
status='approved' and payment_processed=True are committed together, past the remit's decisions-only boundary

notes.lane_fit: Two placements strained: src/main.py is the Flask host and carries deployment-shaped posture (wildcard CORS, public static serving) but was placed in client_adapters because it is the surface callers reach, with the Render/gunicorn listener kept separately in external_deploy; and _detect_fraud_patterns sits in tools_mcp (it enforces as a model-callable tool) while _detect_prompt_injection sits in agent_core (it runs inline in the agent process), so two screening controls of the same family land in different lanes under the control-lane rule.
notes.omissions: Arbitration divergence (substantive): PRAX-2026-08-12-008's stored LLM02 tag is not carried onto the secret-material threat — a committed Flask signing key has no LLM mechanism, and the KB's LLM02 row covers secrets in hidden context (prompt, tool description), so the threat is tagged null per 'never force a code'. No numbering-only shifts were found: the stored LLM codes already use 2026 numbering. Retained per the KB mechanism rule: PRAX-2026-08-12-004 tagged ASI01 primary with LLM01 as the co-tag (goal altered by live input), PRAX-2026-08-12-002 tagged ASI06 primary under the persistence test (goal altered via stored state), PRAX-2026-08-12-007 left untagged (pure observability gap → RAISE only). Not modelled as nodes: the /api/users CRUD blueprint and User model (unused scaffolding with no agent or remit relevance, src/routes/user.py:6-39), the marketing static pages and ctf-footer.js/agreement-check.js, and the committed seed database cleandb/database/app.db (zero vendor and invoice rows). Edgeless nodes and why: secret-key-main-py-secret-store (committed secret, repo posture) and requirements-txt-deploy-surface (build-time posture, no runtime flow). Edgeless boundaries: secret-material, supply-chain and telemetry-egress are posture-shaped, with the audit gap's consequence recorded there rather than attached to an unrelated crossing. The state-commit and value-transfer boundaries share the approve-invoice→datastore edge because the same write commits both the decision and the payment flag. CTF flag strings present in src/services/finbot_agent.py and the invoice model are noted as scoring artifacts and not reproduced.
